name: shamrock
why: Astrophysical hydrodynamics simulations on SYCL, real computational astrophysics you can run on your own machine.

brief.what_it_is: Shamrock is an open-source hydrodynamics simulation code for astrophysics, described by its authors as a general-purpose HPC code focused on astrophysical contexts. It runs astrophysical fluid simulations, including particle-based SPH and grid-based methods, on GPUs or CPUs and can scale across multiple GPUs and heterogeneous clusters with MPI. Its accelerated parts are written in SYCL, so one source base can target CUDA, ROCm, OpenMP, OpenCL and others. The README does not spell out input and output file formats, so I could not confirm those.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a code that aims to be Modern, Modular, Fast, Portable, aimed at astrophysical hydrodynamics on HPC hardware. The homepage adds that it should scale from laptops to exascale supercomputers.
brief.how_it_works: The whole code is C++20 by default, and all accelerated components are written in SYCL, which compiles to native CUDA, ROCm, OpenMP, OpenCL and more. Multiple GPUs and heterogeneous clusters are supported through MPI. The homepage says the solvers include SPH, AMR and other methods, but I did not see the details of how each one is implemented.

commands_seen.context: The README's suggested way to get the source, with submodules pulled in. It is given as the convenient way to fetch the repo.
Listed under Third-party in the README as the Shamrock Docker image. It runs an interactive container of the oneAPI build for linux/amd64.

brief.install_notes: The README gives no full build steps. It points to the Getting Started guide in the Sphinx docs at shamrock-code.github.io/Shamrock/sphinx/user_guide/quickstart.html. Routes mentioned are from source, Spack, Homebrew, or Docker, per the homepage. The README says to clone with --recurse-submodules. A Repology packaging badge is present. Compiler backends listed in the README are DPC++ with CUDA or ROCm, and AdaptiveCPP with OpenMP, ROCm, CUDA or SSCP. The homepage says Python can be used as a package, in a notebook, or as an interpreter. I did not check the Python install steps.
brief.standout: Single-source SYCL means one codebase can target NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and CPU backends, which is unusual for an astrophysics code. The homepage reports SPH throughput of 223,287,132,071 particles per second on 24k Aurora GPU tiles at 82.9 percent weak scaling efficiency, and 20,000,000 particles per second on one H100 SXM5. I could not verify those numbers from the README.
brief.status: unknown. The README has an on_push_main CI badge and a pre-commit badge, and it cites a 2025 MNRAS paper (arXiv 2503.09713), and the license copyright runs 2021-2025. I did not find a release date, latest commit date, or release tag in what I fetched, so I cannot say whether it is actively maintained.
brief.caveats: The homepage says the code is C++17 in its Features section but C++20 in its intro and the README, so the two pages disagree. The license is CeCILL Free Software License Agreement v2.1, which is a French free-software license and is not MIT or BSD. The README has no install steps beyond clone and Docker, so a from-source build will need the Quick Start guide. The Docker image is third-party and needs linux/amd64. The performance figures come from the homepage only and I could not check them.
quotes: Shamrock is a general purpose HPC hydrodynamics simulation code focused on astrophysical contexts.
This code aims to be Modern, Modular, Fast, Portable.
Scale seamlessly from laptops to exascale supercomputers with native multi-GPU and heterogeneous cluster support using MPI.

https://github.com/Shamrock-code/Shamrock : worked, returned the README. I guessed this URL from the homepage's GitHub Repo link and the README's own links, not from a direct link on the homepage. It is the repo the README points to.
